speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, September 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. McMillan that Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as you know, yesterday the clock outran me, not being the athlete that you were in your glory days. I am very pleased, though, to have this opportunity to speak today about legislation which also has inadequate underpinnings and needs a great deal of exercise.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You are not reflecting on the Speaker, are you?

I notice that the Minister is exercising. That is good, because the Act needs a lot of exercise in order to be in shape to do the kind of job which needs to be done.
What we were promised was a gourmet meal; what we have is a stew. That is not adequate. The people of Canada will not think that it is adequate to do the kind of job they want done with the environment, to which they give top priority.
An Act was brought into effect back in 1976 to deal with the environmental impact of chemicals and their effect on human health. Amendments have been under consideration since 1981. The principal concern was that the Act did not adequately provide for the identification and assessment of new chemicals in Canada before they are used and dispersed in the environment.
The Minister has made provision for that in the Act, and we are prepared to accept that it is a good step forward. We support the initiative that new chemicals will be identified, and some will be banned and that action will be taken. We also support the provision that some chemicals now in existence will
be put on the list and will be banned. Those provisions are good ones.
The problem is that we do not know what chemicals will be on the list. Another problem is that the resources devoted to this item are such that it will take a long time before we know. There is a schedule in the Act right now, but it is limited.
In order to go through all the Acts which are coming into this new amalgamation or pot-pourri, it will take a lot of work by a lot of people. The financial allocation to do that work is inadequate to meet the need or do the job. It will be years before the proper chemicals are identified on that list to give adequate protection to the people of Canada.
Therefore we had to question whether the intent is serious when we looked at the resources devoted to doing the kind of job which is talked about in the Act.
In his earlier statements the Minister said that it would deal with all sorts of things. In November, 1985, the St. Clair blob was discovered, and the Minister began promising that the amendment to the Environmental Contaminants Act would somehow clean up the St. Clair River and other existing pollution problems. However, that is not the case. The Minister made that claim repeatedly, but this piece of legislation cannot and will not clean up the Niagara River, the St. Clair River, the waste dumps, and the air pollution from factories. It is not going to do that. It is not going to do the job it was heralded to do in the beginning.
When the Minister released the draft legislation in December he called it the toughest pollution legislation in the western hemisphere. However, by the time he introduced the legislation in the House in June it had diminished to a first step toward cleaning up the environment.
The Minister also promised an environmental bill of rights and instead delivered some elegant prose in the preamble which really has no legal status at all.
There are 24 federal Departments administering 57 environmental laws. The Minister claims that Bill C-74 will streamline that process. Really all that is happening is the merging of three Acts, the Clean Air Act, the Ocean Dumping Control Act and the Environmental Contaminants Act. It is a merging of existing legislation without any change to those Acts at all.
This morning on the way in I heard of an operation yesterday off the East Coast of Newfoundland by the Canadian

September 25, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Coast Guard. It was an experimental cleanup of an oil spill. Oil was dispersed on the water and the Coast Guard tried its technology to see how it would work. It did not work as well as it should have worked. The Coast Guard admitted that there are faults in the technology and faults in the systems in place now to clean up potential spills off the East Coast. That is a very serious situation because the most important resource in my province and the Atlantic provinces is the marine resource. Ironically, the most serious threat to that marine resource is the other greatest potential economic benefit in that area, oil and gas.
There must be protection for our primary marine resource. The marine environment off the Atlantic Coast must be of paramount importance. It must be a priority. The Government must provide through legislation, not just through technology, adequate protection for that most important resource, but that has not been done. There has been no examination of the Ocean Dumping Control Act.
One could make the case that trout and salmon in streams are better protected than the cod off shore. The Fisheries Act is an Act with a lot of strength. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon) has wide-ranging powers to enforce laws regarding the spill of toxic chemicals into rivers. Salmon in their natural habitat are protected.
In my own province, a paper mill was dispersing effluent into the very important Exploits River. The Government worked with the company to ensure that the effluent did not kill the salmon resource in that river. The Fisheries Act allows for certain steps to be taken. It gives the Minister wide-ranging powers to protect the marine resources in rivers. However, that Act does not form a part of this legislation. What does form a part of it is the Ocean Dumping Control Act and that has not been examined, updated, beefed up or given any teeth. Yet we are entering an era in which we hope to develop oil and gas resources off the East Coast.
As I said at the outset, we support the idea that new chemicals will be identified and put on the list and the idea that chemicals already existing will be put on the list in the schedule of the Bill. However, I must repeat that inadequate resources have been allocated by the Government to do that.
As far as we are concerned, some parts of the Bill are objectionable. We find the preamble objectionable. A legislated environmental bill of rights would provide a right to a clean environment and provisions to empower citizens to take action to protect their environment in the courts.
1 noticed that my colleague from British Columbia made the point yesterday that there should be provisions for individuals, for groups and for private citizens to have a part in seeing that the environment is adequately protected. After all, who does the environment belong to? It does not belong to the mining companies or the forestry companies. The environment belongs to the people of Canada. It is their heritage and they have a right to see that it is adequately protected and kept in a proper state for them and their children.
This Bill really does not contain an adequate provision for individuals in local areas to take their responsibilities seriously and to ensure that this Bill and indeed Canada's other environmental laws are properly administered to safeguard their environment. That is a weakness in the Bill.
There are various other weaknesses in the Bill. In our opinion, the Minister missed an opportunity to improve existing legislation that is being rolled into the Environmental Protection Act. I mentioned the Ocean Dumping Control Act already. Some critics argue that the Clean Air Act may in fact have been weakened by its inclusion in the proposed Environmental Protection Act.
As it stands, the Clean Air Act now deals with acid rain and air pollution internationally rather than domestically and domestic emissions are regulated by the same process of toxicity testing and information requirements as other chemicals. Under this regime, one may ask whether or not sulphur dioxide, for example, would qualify as a toxic chemical for regulation by the proposed Environmental Protection Act.
Then there is the question of Ministerial discretion. There are several clauses in the Bill that give the Minister discretion to deal with toxic chemicals. Clause 29(4), for example, would allow the Minister to waive the requirement for any information he decides is unnecessary. Clauses 15 and 16 would allow the Minister, on request of the applicant, to extend the time allowed to meet information requirements or other acts of compliance without public explanation or consultation. Clause 37 would allow the Minister to exempt chemicals from regulation at his discretion.
The Minister has these powers of discretion. If we are to have a law with teeth, there should be a written and clearly expressed intent to ensure that the environment is adequately protected and that those people who are using it, those who are temporary stewards of it, are not allowed to get away with practices that would destroy it for people now living and for their descendants.
There is the question as well of federal-provincial agreements. What we really want to have is a national law with national standards. We know that the provinces have their prerogatives and priorities and we know that everything is not equal across this country. Some provinces must operate in certain ways just to try to maintain equality with other regions of Canada.
The Atlantic Provinces, for example, have to bend over backward to attract industry to the area. I understand the difficulty and the extremes to which one must go to try to create jobs in primary processing. On the other hand, the Government should offer us a national Bill with national standards that is administered without any watering down of jurisdiction. We think it must be very clear that the Government set national standards and enforce and administer them itself.
September 25, 1987

Those are some of the difficulties we have with the Bill. It is an extremely important Bill but it really will not do the kind of job that, first, we were promised it would do, and second, the kind of job that needs to be done in Canada if we are to protect the environment.
We welcome certain provisions in the Bill. It is a step forward but it is not what was promised. It is not adequate. It contains weaknesses that we feel should be improved. We hope the Government will take a second look at it and that the Minister will revise it with a view to trying to do what he said he would do in the beginning, with a view to giving us a good, solid piece of legislation that will do the job that needs to be done.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to hear the Hon. Member endorse this legislation that is designed to protect the environment. We appreciate that the speakers from the Opposition have endorsed this Bill in principle.
The Bill results from consultation which took place, using draft legislation, in December of 1986. Meetings were held right across the country, and written submissions were received as well. Upon reflecting on those meetings and submissions, the Minister made changes. When we took office in 1984 we said we were going to consult with the provinces and individual Canadians and, indeed, we have. We can be very proud of this legislation.
As the Hon. Member indicated, there has been some merging of legislation. He also said that is really all it is. However, it is much more than just that. Bill C-74 is the strongest piece of environmental legislation ever brought before this country. We are very proud of the fact that this Bill has teeth. Offences under this Act will be punished by fines and/or jail sentences.
As well, I hope the Member recognizes the importance of individuals being able to bring complaints to the Minister and the fact the Minister must respond. He talked about the discretion of the Minister, but when 12 people bring forward a complaint about a particular environmental situation the Minister must respond. That is a very important part of the legislation and I hope the Hon. Member will reflect on that fact.
This is not just a merging of legislation. It contains some new and very strong provisions which will indeed protect the environment.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of the Parliamentary Secretary but I do not believe that the teeth she claims are in the Bill, or the process she has alluded to, are adequate. She has said citizens can bring forward complaints and the Minister has to respond. All well and good. Yet we do that every day. We get up for an hour in this House asking questions and the Minister has to respond. That is part of our system and there is nothing really new in it.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
If you apply for a TV licence there is a public hearing. Officials have to sit there and listen to what you have to say. Is this good for the community or bad? How should it be changed? Even with the granting of a TV licence, which is not nearly as important as the protection of the environment, our legislation has at least a minimum of teeth. Yet even that, in my experience, has not always been adequate. There are things we can improve. I am just using this as an example, but the CRTC has to have a series of public hearings where people can come and present their views so we can hear the other side. There is a public process of examination.
We need something that goes beyond simple complaints coming to the Minister to which he has to reply. There have to be stronger provisions for public participation in the process so they can make their views known. Let the officials try and defend themselves. That is the kind of teeth we would like to see in the legislation. This may be a step forward but it is not as large a stride as you used to make, Mr. Speaker, on the football field when you were in your heyday.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Since there are no further questions or comments, debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to speak on this Bill. As the Parliamentary Secretary said, this is probably the strongest environmental Bill brought forward by the Government of Canada. Yet that just indicates the conscious neglect of previous Governments. It certainly does not mean this Bill is adequate.
Canadians are looking for the protection of their total environment. They care about that. They are not looking just for protection against toxic substances. We need a bill of rights to protect the environment. I feel strongly about the fact that we were given stewardship over this planet, but not just to exploit and then destroy. I congratulate the Government on bringing this Bill forward, but it is tragic that it has not shown the necessary leadership and given us a Bill which would really be a bill of rights for the protection of our environment.
I represent an area familiar with these problems. Hamilton Harbour contains many contaminants in its sediment. We know 28 per cent of the fish in the harbour have lip cancer. That fact helps us to recognize the existence of health hazards there. Yet there is nothing in this Bill which says that you as an individual can prove that damage. Yes, a corporation can do it. It looks to commercial protection but not the safety and health of individuals. We feel very strongly that individuals should have the ability to launch a complaint and take action against the people contaminating the environment, whoever that may be. It is important that the legislation be in place so that action can be taken.
Environmental groups should be consulted. We have a wealth of knowledge among people who have devoted many hours of their lives to determine what kind of policy would protect our environment. Yet there is nothing in this Bill that

September 25, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
says those people should be recognized as people who know what they are talking about. We have to care about what happens in our environment here in Canada. We speak of acid rain and other similar problems internationally. Yet we do not really take a strong stand on the issue of how we are destroying our own environment. It is crucial that we look at this and decide there are steps we can take.
We as a Party would love to participate in the process of putting amendments forward to strengthen this Bill. The necessary amendments would allow for public participation, consultation with environmental groups, as well as allowing the individual to complain. As an example, we know how heavily contaminated Hamilton Harbour is. There has been a passing of the buck from one body of government to another. There is nothing in this Bill which strengthens federal powers to clean up and protect the environment.
The Act provides that if you develop cancer from swimming in the Hamilton Harbour and can prove that that is where the cancer came from, you can take action against the Government. Surely we should be looking at prevention rather than taking action after the fact. It is very important that we are able to take action when contaminants are being put into our waters, our air, and our earth rather than waiting until the death sentence has been imposed on people because of that contamination.
The environment has become one of the greatest concerns of the people of Canada. The public is ahead of the politicians and legislators. It is very important that we recognize their desire for a clean environment and to protect this planet so that we can pass on to future generations a legacy of which we can be proud.
We believe strongly that the Act should enable the public to have some influence in the decision-making process. We believe that the powers of the Minister are too broad and can, therefore, be very discriminatory in individual and collective cases. We also believe that there must be a process for discussions with environmental groups. This Bill must enable the people of Canada to take action and be guaranteed protection.
The Bill has consolidated several Acts which could amount to an environmental protection Bill. However, the result has been that some of our environmental protection legislation has been weakened. At this time in our history we need a very strong environmental protection Act. We should be responding to the priorities of Canadians. We must recognize that once the environment is destroyed it is gone forever.
As a result of post-war development we paved over very precious agricultural land. We have bemoaned that tragedy since. A strong environmental protection Act now would keep us from weeping and wailing years from now, saying it is too bad that we did not put some clout into this Act, asking why we did not care enough. I am sure that Members on both sides
of the House have received letters in support of strengthening the Act and ensuring that protection exists so that we will no longer have to apologize for the things which are happening in our environment.
We have contaminated the beautiful Hamilton Harbour and yet we are still not willing to enact legislation to ensure that it is cleaned up. There have been all sorts of recommendations made that we return the Harbour to its previous state in order that people can enjoy it, as our grandparents did. This Act gives us no ability to do that.
We are still talking about preventing toxic substances from entering our environment rather than protecting the environment as a whole or cleaning it up. I find it very difficult to believe that this Bill was drafted without the inclusion of herbicides. We have recognized the danger of the use of herbicides. We know this has harmed health. We have stopped using herbicides in many areas because we were no longer willing to accept the destruction they were causing.
It is also difficult to believe that the Bill does not identify any kind of nuclear substance or radiation. We know that those elements have caused a lot of problems. Research on them is ongoing. Extensive research is being done on low-level radiation. We are very concerned about the genetic problems which they can cause. We know that if the gene bank is destroyed in the human family we will be facing very serious problems.
We should be saying that we care enough about our environment, our country, and our planet that we will not continue on this road of destruction which we have been travelling at a very high speed over the last number of generations. Instead of that we are saying that after destruction has taken place, providing it has caused some type of commercial damage, charges can be laid to stop the destruction, but by then it will be too late.
We know that treatment is much more expensive than prevention. We have the ability to enact a very strong Bill which will protect our environment for many years to come if only we have the political will to do it. We know how people feel about the environment. We know that they care. Therefore, why are we not enacting legislation which will protect the environment for the future?
In conjunction with talking about the environment and this Bill, we must talk about the ability to strengthen federal powers. This has been discussed in the committee on the environment and on the Meech Lake Accord. People have been talking about how we can unify our nation. That is a common goal throughout the country and there is no doubt in my mind that the environment is another.
On this issue the Government can take a strong stand and show the leadership which is so important right now. It can have the courage, which previous Governments did not have, to enact legislation that will really protect the environment, not legislation that will only limit the introduction of toxic
September 25, 1987

substances; a bill of rights for the environment so that people will be protected with ongoing legislation.
We must ensure that people do not have to become terminally ill before they can take action against polluters. It is possible to do these things, but not with this Act. Unless we are willing to accept some amendments that will strengthen the Bill, we are really saying, yes we are ready to give some type of cosmetic support to your concerns about the environment, but we are not ready to take action and say that for us as a nation it is a priority and for us the time has come. Many of us recognize that it is not a case of the time having come, but of the time having long past. We recognize that the time is long past by the type of illnesses we have seen, and when we look at the air that has been so badly polluted.
We have taken some steps in beginning to restrict some of the emissions from our industrial plants. Certainly, I have seen an improvement in the air pollution in Hamilton Mountain, but not to the extent I would like to see. When we have a resource that is as beautiful as the harbour itself, we should recognize that there is nothing in the legislation that would help us clean up that harbour or help us restore it to the state that it was when our grandparents were there, or to make us realize at long last that these are the resources that we can enjoy and use in a very positive manner for future generations.
Citizens must have some type of input, and there must be public participation. Over the years my experience both as a local politician and working on committees has been that very often we get a great sense of knowledge, direction, and problem solving from our communities. The grass roots are living with the problem on a day-to-day basis. They have recommendations and the ability to spend a lot of time and study and know the types of things that are affecting their immediate communities, and the types of things they can do about it.
I do not think that it was the bodies of government or the bureaucrats in the country that brought to the fore the dangers of herbicides. It was the people who were starting to have reactions within their own systems, and who saw the effects on their families and children-they made their presentations. In many cases in the communities across the country they had sit-ins. They refused to let the people spray their parks and their environment. At that point people became aware that there might be a problem with herbicides. We then started to look at the research and recognized that there is a problem.
This is one time when we do have the ability to do something, and not just wait to react. With this Bill we have the ability to put in some strong amendments to make sure it has broad scope, that we do have a bill of rights for the environment, that we do recognize it is the individual's rights that are being eroded by contamination pollutants, and that herbicides and all types of low-level radiation must be recognized as pollutants and contaminants.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
We also must recognize that there is a need for public participation, for consultation with the environmental groups to protect the wealth of resources in this country from the commercial factories that may figure it is too expensive for them to stop polluting and, therefore, they can take a case and defend themselves against it. We must look at what we are attempting to do.
I would hope that the Government recognizes that it is the people of Canada that it wishes to protect, and it is this planet that we have been so blessed with.
I wish to urge the Government to accept some strong amendments to this Bill in order that we who have been part of this legislative body can feel proud in the future to know that we have put some protection there for our children and grandchildren, and to say that we do recognize the beauty of the creativity of this planet.

I wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar). On this side of the House we are very proud, and I am sure her constituents also feel the same when she speaks out so strongly on these issues. I particularly liked the reference of the Hon. Member to a bill of rights for environmental protection.
Coming from the Lower Mainland of Vancouver where we have the beautiful basin of the Fraser River and the Fraser Valley, I was particularly interested in her comment that one of the pollutants we sometimes forget about is blacktop. In our community it is appalling.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I do not wish to interrupt the Hon. Member, but 1 would appreciate it if she would return to her own seat, unless there has been a change in the seating arrangement. I know there have been some changes in the New Democratic Party. If the Hon. Member would return to her seat, I will recognize her again.

Mr. Speaker, I have now returned to my proper place.
I was commenting on the Hon. Member's reference to blacktop as a pollutant, and the fact that in my community of greater Vancouver it is indeed a very vicious pollutant which is covering very lush farmlands and thus depriving us of produce.
In the Hon. Member's community of Hamilton Mountain, and the surrounding area, which is an area I grew up in and certainly recall with fond memories, I wish to ask the Hon. Member if there are any problems concerning the farm lands as far as pollution is concerned, and particularly protections from the acid rain hazards.

I passed over it lightly, but it is important that not only is acid rain destroying our environment on an international basis, but we must be very strict in our own domestic legislation to ensure that the acid rain problem is solved because of what it is doing to our own agriculture. I have seen some of the blight that has happened to the beautiful

September 25, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
orchards in the communities surrounding Hamilton Mountain. It has literally wiped out whole orchards, and it is very serious.
We cannot allude to problems of the environment only on an international basis, and ignore the fact that we do not have the type of strict legislation in this country that would allow us to go to the international forum and talk about what we have implemented to restrict our people from contaminating our environment. In that manner we will have a much stronger voice internationally.
The tragedy that is happening is not only with acid rain, but also with the types of pollutants that have been emitted over the years from industrial plants. We have found that we can put in protection, and the emissions do not need to be at the high level that they have been in the past. Interestingly enough, industrial plants can still produce their products without having to contaminate us. Perhaps the profits may not be quite as high, but they are still adequate, and certainly that will protect the planet for future generations.

I listened with great interest to the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar), and enjoyed what she said. In Toronto there is a harbour and islands. It is quite a few years since I went with my children to swim in the waters off the north shore of Centre Island in Toronto Harbour, and the way it is going I may be able to walk on it before I ever swim in it again.
Toronto City Council has been considering methods of cleaning up the harbour and the Commissioner of Public Works has worked out figures on how many people would be employed in the work that would be necessary to clean it up. However, it is something that is considered rather beyond the budget of even a large city like Toronto.
The question that has been raised is whether the federal Government would help with that clean-up, since it is a harbour and to that degree under federal control. I wonder if there are similar discussions going on in Hamilton about specific plans for cleaning up Hamilton Harbour?
There are many, many recommendations for cleaning up our pollution, and it may be that the public works department of Hamilton has some ideas of what could be done, but less idea of where to find the money. I wonder if the Hon. Member can comment on the question of the funding problem for the cleanup that would be necessary?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, there has been a very clear plan put in place for the clean-up of the harbour. I guess my concern about this Bill is that it does not address any kind of pollutants that are already in place. It talks about toxic substances that are going to be put into the environment but does not talk about any kind of remedial work for pollutants that are already in place.
There have been recommendations from the regional Government of Hamilton-Wentworth, as well as from the
city itself and the province and, certainly, federal representatives. They all agree that it is possible to clean-up the harbour, but one passes the buck to the other and there is no legislation in place stiff enough to say, they have to get on with it because this is a priority. My feeling is that the citizens in the community are saying that they recognize that other things might have to go by the board to clean up our harbour, but they feel it is important enough that they want to enact those kinds of studies and the recommendations that come from those studies.
If we stiffened up this Bill the opportunities would be there to say that action must be taken, and there would be some respect for the citizens of the community. I really think Hamilton deserves this. We deserve to be able to use our harbour the way we could use it. The Hon. Member is right, children can no longer swim in the harbour. If they do, there is danger, and we know what the danger is, we know the health hazards. I really think the opportunity is ours now. We could put in some amendments to this Bill that would give it the kind of strength that would set the priorities, not just for the federal Government, but it would help the municipal and provincial Governments to enact what the priorities are of the people of Hamilton themselves, and the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, although it does not make me particularly happy to say it, I have to note that this is not a Government which has given Canada very strong or effective leadership in dealing with some of our nation's very serious environmental concerns and problems. Although we have a Minister who is very good at political preening and prancing, he has done very little with his responsibilities on a wide range of environmental issues that are of considerable concern to Canadians. I have in mind the control of toxic chemicals and the effect they have on human health. I have in mind acid rain which is causing such drastic damage to the forests in the part of Canada I represent in this House. I am thinking as well of Great Lakes water quality control.
Rather than having done much in the last three years since the Government was elected in terms of positive action towards creating a wholesome, healthy and clean environment, the Government has gone the other way in many cases. For example, we know it has made some very deep cuts to the environmental budget. We know it has ended funding for the Guelph-Toronto Toxicology Research Centre, and we know it has gutted the Canadian Wildlife Service.
I am concerned that the Government is withholding information about what is going on at the renegotiations of the Great Lakes Water Quality Control Agreement. I am concerned because there is clearly a pattern developing, as exemplified by the Meech Lake Accord and by the free trade fiasco, that the Government is quite prepared to give away a great deal and receive very little in return. I am nervous that
September 25, 1987

the Great Lakes Water Control Agreement may be going the same way.
However, in the dying days of the Government we finally get for purposes of debate Bill C-74, an environmental Bill. The Minister dares to describe it as the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. He dares to describe it as a protection Act. We know it is going to do very little to protect the environment. This EPA is really more of an environmental propaganda Act.
A number of very important environmental groups and organizations put out a press release in which they said that Canadians want a real environmental protection Act, that the content of the proposed Act does not merit the title "Canadian Environmental Protection Act". The federal Government must assert its responsibility to protect the environment for its own sake. This group went on to say that Canadians put protection of the environment at the top of their priorities and it is time this Government did the same.
1 agree with the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) who delivered an impressive speech this morning. I agree with her that Canadians want, expect and deserve very strong action from their federal Government in terms of protecting the environment. They want an environmental protection Act, but I would argue that what they are getting in Bill C-74 is really an environmental deception Act.
As 1 said, this is the first time we have had the Government bring forward a Bill regarding the environment which was debatable. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill is not much. Whenever the House has turned its attention in the last three years to questions about the environment and the state it is in, it has usually been because motions have been brought forward by one or the other of the Opposition Parties. That is when we have had vigorous debate in this House on the environment.
As you know, Sir, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), has been very diligent and vigorous in the defence of a clean environment, whether air, water or land. He has become Canada's best known watchdog on the environment. He is a respected individual who regularly brings to the attention of this Parliament our fears and concerns about the environment. In contrast to that, we have a Minister who eulogizes, sermonizes and stage manages concerns about the environment. All of that gives us very little in the way of any forward movement.
You are signalling, Mr. Speaker, that we are going to the next stage of our proceedings. I will complete my remarks when we resume debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the Ontario Provincial Court last May the Bank of Canada, the National Research Council, the Department of Transport, and the Department of Supply and Services were accused of breaking the law by dumping toxic waste into the Ottawa River. We have learned this week that charges against these departments and agencies have been tossed out because the environment protection legislation does not apply to the federal Government. The very fact that it does not abide by its own legislation goes to show to what extent the Conservative Government could not care less about the rights of Canadian men and women to live in a pollution-free environment.
How can this Government condone environmental pollution while at the same time spending $74 million under a tripartite agreement aimed at cleaning up the Ottawa River? Last June the federal Government tabled a legislative measure which is designed to protect the environment, human life and health and which is so severe that it provides life terms and unlimited fines in cases of crimes against the environment. If all Canadians are to be subject to the proposed legislation, so should the Canadian Government.

Mr. Speaker, this week is Planned Parenthood Week and the theme is "Your sexuality lasts a lifetime: Make it healthy". President Norma Buchan states:
With the current public focus on the negative aspects of sexual activity such as unplanned pregnancy and the spread of AIDS and other sexually-transmitted diseases, a positive health-oriented approach to sexuality is more important than ever. Education and awareness are the first steps to a healthier sexual life-style.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. McMillan that Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, earlier today I was making some comments on Bill C-74, the Bill which the Government calls the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, though I believe that to be a misnomer. However, I had not completed my remarks when we moved to Statements by Members and Question Period.
At that time, I was pointing out to the House that this is the first environmental Bill to be introduced in the House for debate by this Government in its three years in office.
In the fall of 1985, nearly two years ago, the so-called St. Clair River blob came to public attention. At that time the Minister, responding to concerns raised by environmental leaders throughout Canada and to questions raised in the House by Members of Parliament, said that he planned to bring in an environmental contaminants Act which would clean up this foul, putrid mess. He said that it would do more than that, that it would solve other problems as well. He told us that we could expect that this planned legislation would deal with matters relating to the Niagara River, that there would be legislation which would help us deal with old waste dumps and that something would be forthcoming to deal with the pollutants that pour forth from a variety of factories across Canada.
In December of 1985, the Minister put forward a Bill which we did not debate. In his vain fashion, he called the Bill the toughest pollution legislation in the western world. That Bill died on the Order Paper, and the following June another Bill was introduced. This time the tough guy lines that had been scripted for the Minister had to be changed and we got a different story. Instead of the toughest pollution legislation in the western world, this time we got just a first step toward

September 25, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
cleaning up the environment. We went from tough guy to timid first step in a matter of a couple of months.
NoxV Bill C-74 is before us. This morning, the Parliamentary Secretary was back using tough guy words once more. However, we know that those words really do not apply to Bill C-74. Later on I will bring to the attention of the House some evidence supporting that charge.
Bill C-74 is the merging of some legislation that has been around for quite a while. It merges the Clean Air Act, the Ocean Dumping Control Act and the Environmental Contaminants Act. These Acts have been brought together for streamlining, as described by the Minister. However, a spokesman for the Alberta group of the Sierra Club of western Canada has written the following:
We feel that this proposal is not a complete environmental protection act as it leaves out important areas such as acid rain, motor vehicle emissions, recycling of wastes, hazardous goods movement, protection of flora and fauna, and a host of other very important factors in protecting Canada's environment. The Act should be renamed.
At one point in his career, the Minister spoke in the vainglorious terms, for which he is famous, of an environmental bill of rights. That is a lovely bit of sermonizing, a bill of rights based on environmental concerns. Of course, there is nothing close to a bill of rights in Bill C-74. Instead, there is a preamble to the legislation itself. The theme of the preamble is the environment. It is a prissy little piece on protecting the environment and human health.
We all know what a preamble is all about. On certain occasions in a court of law it may help the interpretation if there has been bad or vague drafting of the legislation. However, for the most part, a preamble has no legal status at all. It is usually just a bit of propaganda and exists for decorative purposes. It is a cosmetic that disguises reality.
What is the reality? The reality is that there is very little in the way of new action on environmental control in Bill C-74. In support of this argument, I quote Toby Vigod, a lawyer working with the Canadian Environmental Law Association:
-the preamble to the proposed EPA is not legally enforceable. Case law and authorities on the subject of preambles generally conclude that they are not enforceable in and of themselves. They, however, can be used as a limited aid to interpretation in determining the meaning of statutory provisions that may be unclear and ambiguous.
I hope that the Minister has not given us a Bill which is unclear and ambiguous, but if he has, then perhaps his little preamble will be helpful in certain cases. Vigod goes on to conclude the following:
However, this does not confer rights on citizens to protect their environment.
Let me turn to another source to support my argument. Pollution Probe has described this environmental Bill as being meaningless. Pollution Probe has said, as reported by the Ottawa Citizen:
Environment Minister Tom McMillan's claim to have produced the country's first environmental bill of rights is meaningless, a Pollution Probe spokesman says.
Janine Ferretti said in an interview from Toronto that if McMillan had wanted to include an enforceable bill of rights in his draft Environmental Protection Act, unveiled this week, he wouldn't have put it in the preamble of the new legislation where it has no legal basis.
Since there is no bill of rights at all, we do not need to talk about that any longer.
It has been said that this Bill does some streamlining. I challenge that as well. I do not think much has been streamlined when there are still 24 departments of Government responsible for 55 different statutes that deal in one way or another with environmental matters.
To be fair, Bill C-74 does one useful thing. It sets up a system that will assess the impact of new chemicals that come on to the market on human health and the environment. That was a task begun but not completed under the previous Government. However, my concern is that there will not be enough resources available to adequately do that important task. We know that there is a very fixed and restrained budget in the Department to help it undertake this task.
I want to agree with my friend from Newfoundland and Labrador when he says it is time the Ocean Dumping Control Act was given new force. You may have read, Sir, that the Act, brought in by the previous Government, is now being challenged in the Supreme Court. Here was a chance for the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) to add new force to that Act, but he did not. He just folded it into C-74.
1 fear, as does my hon. friend from Newfoundland and Labrador who spoke earlier in the debate, that the Clean Air Act as encompassed in C-74 may possibly-we cannot say categorically-permit sulphur dioxide to slip underneath the existing regulations and escape control altogether. That is so because, as the Parliamentary Secretary knows, acid rain is to be subject to the same toxicity test as other chemicals. So you can see that sulphur dioxide may escape altogether.
In addition, the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) also asked whether C-74 gives the Minister too much discretionary power. I wonder, and other Members wonder, should he be allowed to exempt chemicals from regulation altogether simply at his discretion?
Undoubtedly Bill C-74 is weakened by allowing each and every province to have a veto over the legislation if they feel- not if they prove but if they feel-that they have legislation of their own comparable to this legislation. I would ask, who is going to be the judge of that? No, I think C-74 suffers from what I would call the Meech Lake blights. I quote The Toronto Star.
Specifically, two sections in the bill before Parliament would require McMillan to consult all the provinces before he drafts regulations or issues emergency orders to control toxic chemicals.
While Ottawa would retain the right to act on its own after the consultations, the provisions invite Ottawa to take the weakest possible action, so that everyone can agree.
September 25, 1987

In sharp contrast to that, Sir, the Brundtland report says what is really needed is strong national standards enforced on a national basis. In my view, that is what Canada desperately needs and that is borne out of the kind of federalism that we are gradually negotiating away day by day.
I want to conclude by pointing out that the Parliamentary Secretary made the argument earlier today that this was a tough piece of legislation, the toughest we have ever seen. I want to quote from The Financial Post, an article by Doug Hunter who says:
The Canadian Environmental Protection Act, tabled in Parliament on June 26, talks tough, with million-dollar-a-day fines against polluters and provisions for jailing executives of offending companies. CEOs probably won't be marching off to jail in leg irons, though, unless their pollution is accompanied by such gross misbehaviour as fraud, obstruction of inspectors or the death of innocent bystanders.
Environmentalists criticize the act for its failure to set broad national standards, particularly for water quality.
"It's Swiss cheese with fewer holes," says Toby Vigod, a lawyer and clinic director of the Canadian Environmental Law Association. "If I was in industry, I wouldn't be particularly perturbed. It's not going to affect day-today business."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words in response to what the Hon. Member said concerning Bill C-74. He mentioned the Brundtland report. That report was prepared by a committee chaired by Prime Minister Brundtland of Norway. We were very pleased with it. Indeed, this House unanimously endorsed it a few months ago.
The Minister set up a task force of environment Ministers which met as recently as the last two days in Quebec City. That task force was set up five months after the World Commission on Environment and Development warned that environmental problems on this planet are approaching crisis levels. Our task force was to respond to that report as it looks at how the world is going to have to view environmental issues. I would like to quote from a Globe and Mail article of yesterday which said:
Mr. MacNeill, who was secretary-general to the Brundtland commission, said no other country is as advanced as Canada in dealing with the recommendations of the world commission.
Not only are we getting recognition from around the world for our outstanding contribution in this area, let us look specifically at the acid rain abatement programs which the Member talked about. We have made an outstanding contribution in reducing acid rain. We have reached agreements on reducing sulphur dioxide emissions. We are getting our House in order. We are now into very difficult negotiations with the U.S., but we heard on the floor of this House the President of the United States talking about an accord on this issue. Just last week we had the Montreal protocol on the ozone. Our Minister of the Environment took a very strong leadership position in getting that protocol. We have produced automobile emission standards which will lead to the phasing out of
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
leaded gasoline. Indeed, there are many other examples which show the great accomplishments of this Government in cleaning up the environment.
Bill C-74 is another example. We are looking at chemicals coming on to the market, controlling those chemicals, producing priority lists, and putting teeth in the legislation in the form of penalties for those who pollute the environment. I think we should congratulate the Government on its fine work.

Mr. Speaker, you will know, as I do, that there is a world of difference between Setting up a task force on a report which is as significant, useful and pointed as the Brundtland rep'Ort is, and actually carrying out recommendations. One of the recommendations in the Brundtland report is that a nation requires a central authority for pollution control. If you decentralize pollution legislation and control and authority, the chances of getting effective pollution law and action is diminished. That is one of the messages in the Brundtland report.
When the Government tells us it has accepted that report and is going to take its responsibilities seriously, that we are going to have effective environmental protection law, then we will sit up and pay attention. However, when the Parliamentary Secretary talks about another task force we on this side are not very convinced.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, you asked Whether the House was ready for the question. We on this side; of the House are certainly not ready for the question. I am a little surprised that Members of the Government did not take the opportunity to enter this debate. I am surprised that they are not sufficiently concerned about environmental matters to elaborate upon the policies that the Government has chosen to legislate.
They reacted in a very negative way to the critical comments made by my colleague to my right. They reacted very defensively when he criticized the inadequacies of the legislation before the House. They reacted to his criticisms with a minute-long question. I would have appreciated a much more extensive and thorough response. I would have appreciated the comprehensive and in-depth debate which is required.
This Chamber is set up with the Opposition on one side of the room and the Government on the other. That encourages adversarial discussions which have merit. However, in addition to the Opposition blaming the Government and the Government advertising its own merits we need a thorough and profound debate on environmental questions. I invite members of the Government to enter that debate. I invite them to share with the public the thinking, if any, that they have done on environmental questions.

September 25, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
I am obviously not going to pretend that I do not enjoy pointing out weaknesses in the Government's legislation when they exist and need to be pointed out. However, I do invite members of the Government to enter this fundamental and serious debate, which is a watershed debate.
It was not so long ago that we would not be having a debate about environmental protection or health as related to environmental matters. It would have been taken for granted that the supreme value was economic development of any kind at any cost. We would have assumed that the planet could sustain any efforts at economic growth, that the earth could recover from any pollution and damage to the environment, and we could continue merrily on our way.
Over the last number of decades we have become much more aware of the seriousness of environmental matters. There are serious questions on survival for the planet and the human species and on the equality of our life. The vast majority of the general public is becoming aware of these matters.
We are establishing new bottom lines with regard to the environment. We are establishing new standards and new expectations on the environment. People are no longer willing to put up with the old economic blackmail of companies saying that if they are required to meet environmental standards they will have to close plants and do away with the jobs. Such economic blackmail has been going on for years and has made governments afraid to set the necessary standards to preserve the environment. The ultimate threat against a government is that of pulling out investment which will cause the loss of jobs, and thereby the loss of votes and office.
That game was played effectively until now. However, there is an emerging new consciousness on environmental matters. The politics of the environment and the economy are in the process of changing and we must recognize that. Of course new standards for environmental protection put limits on economic growth and development. However, it is implicit in creativity that you have some limits. A creative person is not free to do anything he or she wishes. A creative country recognizes the limits and then, within those limits, does that which needs to be done.
We must ask ourselves how we can develop our economy and have economic growth and employment as well as environmental protection. How can we have a good, safe, clean, healthy environment and employment as well? We must stop accepting the false dichotomy that the choice is between environmental protection and employment. We must say no to industries that want a licence to pollute. One way of learning to say no to that kind of blackmail from industry is to develop new types of economic development which will respect the environment.
If we do not find new methods of economic development which are environmentally sound, we will have no economic development at all. When all the rivers and forests are destroyed by acid rain there will be no employment and no economics at all. It is a very narrow perspective which says
that we must choose between environmental protection and employment. We must broaden that perspective. We must lean how to develop the economy in ways which will respect the environment.
I would like to address Bill C-74 specifically. As we set out our goal of a safe environment and a dynamic economy we must figure out how to achieve it. Does the legislation before the House today contribute to moving toward such a society? The legislation does make some progress toward environmental protection. I do not want to be entirely negative about what the Government is doing, but I do want to point out the shortcomings as they must be pointed out. While this is a step forward, it is only a small step. It is a disappointing step. Much more needs to be done, and much more could have been done.
One of the most shocking things about this legislation is the manner in which it was drafted. It was drafted behind closed doors in somebody's closet. Rather than having comprehensive public hearings involving the citizens of Canada and those groups that monitor the environment and seek to protect it for the rest of us, and having them assist in drafting the legislation and setting the new standards, the Government goes behind closed doors and drafts the legislation. That is a major discrepancy and serious weakness with the legislation.
It is clear that we cannot arrive at a point where there is strong, sound environmental legislation unless we involve the public and inform the citizens of the process of developing that legislation. We are involved in a process of creating a new political culture, and setting new standards of conduct affecting the environment. That is a democratic process which requires the will and the support of the people. It cannot be done behind closed doors, it must be done in a public environment. That is one of the first weaknesses of the legislation and the process.
Another problem and major criticism of the legislation is that it does not include an environmental bill of rights. The Government has spoken glowingly about its legislation. Of course, we expect it to do that. We would like to hear more from the government side of the House in this debate. While it speaks glowingly of the legislation, it does not include an environmental bill of rights.
It is important to acknowledge that people have a right to a healthy environment. It is not some privilege, but it is a fundamental human right. It is important to have a safe and healthy environment because human beings cannot survive and reach their potential without a healthy and safe environment that is non-polluted. This is a matter of human rights. I know that it is a new concept to consider a non-polluted environment as a matter of human rights. It is a more familiar concept to think of human rights as concerning matters of race and discrimination. We are not yet familiar with the notion of the environment as a human right, but fundamentally it is, because in order to live and grow and reach full potential a
September 25, 1987

human being must have a safe, healthy and non-polluted environment.
What else are we referring to when we talk about an environmental bill of rights? One of the central points made by environmental groups is that the public must have an opportunity to be involved in this process and play a role in the enforcement of environmental law. Why are those groups asking for ordinary citizens to have the right to play a role in entorcing environmental standards? Surely when we pass legislation in the Elouse establishing environmental standards, that means there will be an end to pollution. We will stop laying waste to our environment. It should not be necessary for an ordinary citizen in my riding to become involved in the process in order to ensure that these standards are met.
The problem is that environmental legislation is often window dressing. While Governments have good standards on the books, they allow a great deal of discretion for their Ministers of the Environment and Cabinet. We may have good statements of commitments from Ministers, and we may have good standards written into legislation, there tend to be loopholes in these situations and Governments have failed to carry out these standards with the vigour required. When it comes to the environment, Governments tend to follow behind public opinion. Citizens feel that they cannot trust their Governments. Government continues to allow the environment to be polluted and succumbs to economic blackmail. Therefore, citizens feel that it cannot be left to the politicians, they have to become involved. They must have a legal right to be involved in the process because Governments fail to follow through. That is what we mean when we talk about an environmental bill of rights.
Another key point in regard to an environmental bill of rights is the fact that citizens should have some right to participate in environmental decision-making. The Minister has the right to set standards and to outline what levels industries have to meet, but the public must have an opportunity to be involved with regard to the establishment of standards. That cannot be left to the Ministers alone.
Some serious criticisms have been brought forward in this legislation. I am not only making these criticisms to make the Government look bad. I must say that sometimes the impression is that the Government invites that to be done. I am not doing this only to be negative because I am on the opposition side and my friends are on the government side. 1 am doing this because it is important for us to realize that public opinion is ahead of public policy. When it comes to the environment, up until the present time Canadian citizens have had much higher standards than public policy indicates.
The legislation before us today takes some steps forward, but those steps are feeble compared to what the public is demanding and what the public will support. Canadians are asking Governments to set a new bottom line when it comes to the environment, and to say, "No more polluting the environment, no more laying waste to the environment, no more acid
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
rain, no more building of nuclear plants and building up wastes that we do not know how to handle which will be a problem for unforeseen generations. No more creating problems that are a danger to human health and survival".
The public is out in front and needs decisive and strong action from Governments. We need the Government to represent the people and to say that we will no longer allow the environment to be laid waste by industry as a result of economic blackmail. Governments should be creative in the manner in which they handle economic development and preserve the environment.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have a few comments on the allegations made by the socialist Member who said no Conservative Members rose today on this matter. I would remind him that six Government Members have already spoken, that this Government has had a day and half of debate on this legislation, that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is impatiently awaiting the House's acceptance of the Bill on second reading, so that it can be referred to a committee where it will be very well scrutinized.
I would also like to tell him that, as far as relations with industry and environment protection are concerned, he is not so well abreast of the situation because he should read the report presented yesterday, September 24, to the National Council of Resources and Environment Ministers. That report of the Council chaired by no other than Mr. Gerald Lecuyer, a socialist from Manitoba, has this to say in its introduction: "This report includes ideas and recommendations to harmonize Canada's sustained economic development with its environment". So we do not have that many lessons to receive from the socialist Member concerning any harmonization between environment protection and the industrial community.
Finally, he blames us for acting alone in the discussion of this Bill.
First, I would like to point out that it is very difficult to cooperate with the socialists. However, we have not acted unilaterally. There have been many public meetings about this Bill. The Bill itself has been published and fully explained. Minister have made speeches throughout Canada. There have been meetings at the provincial level.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, it is important to remind the House that the Hon. Member is able to speak about the environment today simply because his leader was unsuccessful in obtaining a debate on free trade. He objected to having such a debate for two and a half years, but he asked for one today. Now, he wants to fill the gap because the Chair refused the NDP request for this debate, with good reason, as it would have been quite inconsistent with everything the socialists have said for the past two and a half years. If the Hon. Member wants to go on wasting taxpayers' money and the time of this House, he can do so, but we of the Conservative party have done our duty

September 25, 1987
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
by preparing a good Bill. They should now shut up. This is what more and more Canadians are asking them to do.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to reply to my capitalist friend across the aisle. I should like to add that this capitalist colleague of mine says his caucus has taken part in this debate. However, I have noted today that not one Conservative Member has asked to speak before me. A Liberal Member spoke but afterwards, not a sound was heard from the benches of the capitalist Conservative Members. I want to hear the great capitalists in this House. Mr. Speaker, I want the legislation to be improved. If you want this legislation to be passed by the House, you have to take part in the debate and state your reasons. This is the intent of the House. However, my capitalist colleague said that the Minister from Manitoba, our Minister of the Environment, talked about the harmony that exists between environment and industry. It is true. This is the value we are advocating in this House but no harmony achieved at any cost. We should be ready to set standards so that the industry will not keep on polluting the environment.
I should like to reply to the comments of my capitalist colleague on free trade.
I am against free trade if this new committment, if any, will reduce our environmental standards in Canada to the same level as in the United States where the President will not acknowledge the problem of acid rain.
With respect to acid rain, 1 should like to know if my capitalist friend agrees with the President of the United States, Mr. Ronald Reagan. Is it the reason why he supports the free trade concept?
